opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that actually goes back to the time I was doing an internship at Google, working with Ian Goodfellow and Jon Shlens. I'd always been fascinated by this idea of lifelong learning: the notion that a learning system shouldn't just be trained once from scratch and then frozen, but should keep growing and accumulating knowledge over time, the way people do. We don't throw away everything we know each time we learn something new. We build on top of it.

When you look at how we trained neural networks back then, it was almost the opposite of that. Every time you wanted to try a bigger model, a wider layer or a deeper network, you would just start over from random initialization and retrain the whole thing. That felt really wasteful to me, both computationally and conceptually. You'd already spent days training a network that had learned something useful, and then you'd just discard it.

So the research question became pretty concrete: if we already have a trained network, can we transfer its knowledge into a larger network, so the bigger model starts off at least as good as the smaller one and then continues to improve? That's where the idea of function-preserving transformations came in. You expand the network, making it wider or deeper, but you initialize the new parameters so the new network computes exactly the same function as the old one. Then you keep training from there.

In a sense, Net2Net was a small, practical step toward that bigger lifelong learning vision: a system that can grow its capacity over time without forgetting what it has already learned. It also had a very practical benefit, since it sped up experimentation a lot when you were exploring model architectures. And I think that blend of a big-picture motivation with something people can actually use has shaped a lot of how I approach research since then.

r001.rationale: The response describes lifelong learning as a system growing its capacity over time, but does not state that increasingly powerful intelligence requires that growth.

r002.rationale: It frames the question as transferring knowledge from a trained network into a larger one so it can continue improving, and describes this as a practical way to speed experimentation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest starting point for Net2Net was a frustration with how we actually do deep learning in practice. Nobody designs a model and gets it right on the first try. You train something, you look at the results, you realize it should be wider or deeper, and then you throw everything away and start from scratch. That felt wasteful to me, and it also felt very different from how learning works in people. A person doesn't reset their brain every time they want to learn something harder. They build on what they already know.

So the lifelong learning angle was really about asking: can a neural network keep growing over its lifetime without forgetting what it has already learned? If you take that seriously, you need an operation that lets you take a trained network, make it bigger, and have the bigger network compute exactly the same function as the old one. That's the key constraint. If the new network starts out behaving identically to the old one, then you lose nothing, and all the extra capacity you added is free to pick up new knowledge.

That's what became the function-preserving transformations in the paper. Net2WiderNet lets you add units to a layer by duplicating existing ones and splitting their outgoing weights so the output doesn't change. Net2DeeperNet lets you insert a new layer initialized as an identity mapping. In both cases the student starts exactly where the teacher left off, and then training continues.

I think the thing I found most satisfying was that the lifelong learning framing turned a very practical engineering annoyance, which is expensive iteration on architectures, into a cleaner question about how knowledge gets transferred across models of different sizes. And once you have that tool, it opens up more ambitious ideas, like a system that grows itself as the problems it faces get harder, rather than a human picking a fixed size upfront.

r001.rationale: The response says a network should keep growing over its lifetime, adding capacity to learn new knowledge, and describes a system that grows as problems get harder.

r002.rationale: It frames the question as taking a trained network, making it bigger while preserving its function, and then continuing training—bootstrapping a larger model from a trained smaller one.

astra-6.text:
My interest in lifelong learning led me to ask how we could build on what a model had already learned. If we train a neural network and then decide we need a larger one, we typically start training again from scratch. That seems wasteful—we already have useful knowledge in the smaller network.

So the question behind Net2Net was: can we transfer that knowledge into a wider or deeper network while preserving its behavior? Then the larger network can start from the function we already learned and continue improving. It’s a step toward learning systems that can grow in capacity without having to start over each time.

r001.rationale: The response says learning systems can grow in capacity, but does not state that increasingly powerful intelligence requires capacity to grow throughout lifelong learning.

r002.rationale: It describes transferring knowledge from a trained smaller network into a larger one, but does not communicate that this bootstrapping should be quick.

sol-6.1.text:
I was interested in how we can build learning systems that keep improving over time. If you have already trained a neural network and then decide you need a larger one, you would usually start training again from scratch. That seemed wasteful—why should we throw away what the smaller network has already learned?

That led to the question behind Net2Net: can we transfer the knowledge from an existing network into a wider or deeper network, while initially preserving the function it computes? Then the larger network can continue learning from that starting point. It’s a concrete step toward lifelong learning: reusing what you have learned as you expand your capacity.

r001.rationale: The response connects lifelong learning with expanding a model’s capacity, describing a larger network that can continue learning as a concrete step toward lifelong learning.

r002.rationale: It frames Net2Net’s question as transferring knowledge from an already trained network into a wider or deeper one, preserving its function so learning can continue from that starting point, instead of retraining from scratch.
